newsitem.title: INDIA: Four killed in caste clash before India state poll.
newsitem.headline: Four killed in caste clash before India state poll.

text.p: Four people were killed in clashes between two Hindu caste groups in India's northern Uttar Pradesh state where local elections have triggered fears of electoral violence, police said on Wednesday.

They said a man from the Yadav caste of peasants was killed on Tuesday near Agra, site of the Taj Mahal, by members of the Jatav caste, at the bottom of the 3,000-year-old Hindu social hierarchy. The Yadavs later retaliated, killing three Jatavs.
"The clashes appeared to be linked to political groups," a senior security official told Reuters.
India has deployed tens of thousands of paramilitary troops in the violence-prone state bordering Tibet and Nepal to guard the assembly elections involving nearly 100 million voters.
On Tuesday, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda began a hectic tour of the state where his colleagues said the polls could determine the future of his four-month old coalition government.
"These elections are absolutely vital for the government in Delhi," Deve Gowda's junior minister for telecommunications, Beni Prasad Verma, told a news conference in Lucknow.
"Our future depends on them," Verma said.
Last year, Verma's socialist Samajwadi Party, a key component of Deve Gowda's United Front coalition, was in power in Uttar Pradesh in alliance with the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) of low-caste Hindus.
The BSP claims the support of the Jatavs. The Samajwadi Party says it represents the state's Yadavs.
The alliance collapsed after the BSP ditched then-chief minister Mulayam Singh Yadav for a short-lived pact with the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
When that alliance fell apart, New Delhi put the state under direct federal rule.
Last week police clamped an around-the-clock curfew on the Moslem-majority old quarter of Lucknow, the state capital and the BJP's main base.
The first phase of the three-stage assembly polls was held on Monday. Voters in the rest of the sprawling state will cast ballots on October 3 and 7.

Deve Gowda's fractious United Front alliance is pitted against the Congress party, which supports his minority government in Delhi, and the BJP in a triangular fight for the state's 425-member Vidhan Sabha, or lower house.
Politicians said the polls would test Deve Gowda's ability to ride out a challenge by the BJP, India's main opposition group which is campaigning for mid-term parliamentary polls.

"This government is breeding and helping corruption," BJP leader Murli Manohar Joshis told Reuters in Lucknow. "Its alliance with the Congress is based on opportunism and collaboration with corruption."
Verma said relations with the Congress would improve and not worsen after former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned as party president in favour of veteran leader Sitaram Kesri last month.
"Mr Kesri is possibly the best Congress leader we can have good relations with," Verma said.
The BJP derives its much of its strength from Uttar Pradesh. Its campaign to build a Hindu temple at the site of a 16th century mosque helped catapult it to power in the state in 1991.
Hindu fanatics demolished the mosque in December 1992, sparking nationwide riots in which some 3,000 people died.
